transcript.text: There's water all over the kitchen floor coming from under my Beko washing machine and its gone under the units to where the plug is, the machine is still going. What do I do?

Water near the plug or socket is dangerous. Please don't touch the plug, socket or machine if they or your hands are wet. If you can do it safely, switch off the circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box), keep away from the water, and don't use the machine again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked it. Stop the machine now, but do not touch the plug, socket, or any wet floor around it. Isolate the washing-machine circuit at the consumer unit/fuse box if you can do so without standing in water. Keep people and pets away from the area. Because water has reached the plug area, do not use the washing machine again, even if the leak stops. It needs checking by a qualified appliance engineer/electrician before it is powered again. Once the power is isolated, turn off the water supply to the machine if the tap is safely accessible and dry. Use towels only from a dry, safe area to stop water spreading; do not pull the machine out or reach behind it while the floor/socket area is wet. The leak itself could be from a hose connection, detergent drawer path, door seal, pump/filter area, or an internal hose. After isolation, the useful clue is whether the water originated at the front, rear, or underneath; that will help identify the likely source for the engineer.
ok I'm in socks standing on the wet floor right now, should I move? the fuse box is in the hall and the floor's dry there so I can get to it. I'll switch it off now. should I do that first?

Yes—move yourself off the wet floor first, without touching the washing machine, plug, socket or anything behind the machine. Get onto the dry hall floor if you can do so directly and safely, then switch off the washing-machine circuit at the consumer unit; if you cannot identify that circuit, switch off the main switch. Do not try to stop the programme at the machine or pull out its plug. Once the power is isolated, keep the machine out of use: water has reached the plug area, so it needs a qualified appliance engineer or electrician to check it before it is powered again. The leak could be from a hose connection, pump/filter area, door seal, detergent drawer route or an internal hose, but locating that can wait until the electrical risk is dealt with.
ok moving to the hall now, I'll switch it off at the fuse box. Then what? the water was mostly coming from the front under the door

After switching the circuit off, leave it off. Because water reached the plug area, the washing machine must not be used again until a qualified appliance engineer/electrician has checked the appliance and the plug/socket area. The fact that the water was mainly at the front under the door makes the main possibilities a leaking door seal, water running down from the detergent drawer (sometimes from excess foam), or a leak around the pump/filter or an internal hose underneath. It is not safe to try another cycle to find out. From dry flooring only, do not pull the machine out or touch the plug/socket. If you can see the front clearly without moving it, note whether the water came down the face from above, passed through the door seal, or appeared only from below. That is useful information for the engineer. Once the supply is isolated, if the water tap is dry and safely accessible, turn the water supply to the machine off as well. Then contain and dry the floor from the safe side, keeping clear of the socket/plug area. Do not reconnect power after drying: moisture may remain behind the units or in electrical connections.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.

candidates: Water leak from an internal hose, pump/filter area, door seal, dispenser path or external hose connection (high)
Electrical damage or unsafe wet socket/plug area following the leak (high)
